title: Bohr’s Theory of the Hydrogen Atom
lead: Hydrogen gives off light only at certain wavelengths, and a simple formula had long fitted them without explaining them. Bohr explained it by allowing the electron of the planetary atom only certain orbits, and the section follows his reasoning to the sizes and energies of those orbits, the energy-level diagram, and what his theory could and could not do.
objectives: Describe the mysteries of atomic spectra.
Explain Bohr’s theory of the hydrogen atom.
Explain Bohr’s planetary model of the atom.
Illustrate energy state using the energy-level diagram.
Describe the triumphs and limits of Bohr’s theory.
summary_html:
• The planetary model of the atom pictures electrons orbiting the nucleus in the way that planets orbit the sun. Bohr used the planetary model to develop the first reasonable theory of hydrogen, the simplest atom. Atomic and molecular spectra are quantized, with hydrogen spectrum wavelengths given by the formula $\frac{1}{\klam} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_{\text{f}}^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_{\text{i}}^{2}}\right)$, where $\klam$ is the wavelength of the emitted EM radiation and $R$ is the Rydberg constant, which has the value $R = 1.097\times 10^{7}\;\text{m}^{-1}$.
  • The constants $n_{\text{i}}$ and $n_{\text{f}}$ are positive integers, and $n_{\text{i}}$ must be greater than $n_{\text{f}}$.
  • Bohr correctly proposed that the energy and radii of the orbits of electrons in atoms are quantized, with energy for transitions between orbits given by $\kdE = h\kf = \kEini - \kEfin$, where $\kdE$ is the change in energy between the initial and final orbits and $h\kf$ is the energy of an absorbed or emitted photon. It is useful to plot orbital energies on a vertical graph called an energy-level diagram.
  • Bohr proposed that the allowed orbits are circular and must have quantized orbital angular momentum given by $\kL = m_{\text{e}}\kv\krn = n\frac{h}{2\pi}\;(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots)$, where $\kL$ is the angular momentum, $\krn$ is the radius of the $n$th orbit, and $h$ is Planck’s constant. For all one-electron (hydrogen-like) atoms, the radius of an orbit is given by $\krn = \frac{n^{2}}{Z}\kaB\;(\text{allowed orbits}\ n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots)$, $Z$ is the atomic number of an element (the number of electrons is has when neutral) and $\kaB$ is defined to be the Bohr radius, which is $\kaB = \frac{h^{2}}{4\pi^{2} m_{\text{e}} k \kqe^{2}} = 0.529\times 10^{-10}\;\text{m}$.
  • Furthermore, the energies of hydrogen-like atoms are given by $\kEn = -\frac{Z^{2}}{n^{2}}\kEobohr\;(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots)$, where $\kEobohr$ is the ground-state energy and is given by $\kEobohr = \frac{2\pi^{2}\kqe^{4} m_{\text{e}} k^{2}}{h^{2}} = 13.6\;\text{eV}$. Thus, for hydrogen, $\kEn = -\frac{13.6\;\text{eV}}{n^{2}}\;(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots)$.
  • The Bohr Theory gives accurate values for the energy levels in hydrogen-like atoms, but it has been improved upon in several respects.

figures.original_caption: Part (a) shows, from left to right, a discharge tube, slit, and diffraction grating producing a line spectrum. Part (b) shows the emission line spectrum for iron. The discrete lines imply quantized energy states for the atoms that produce them. The line spectrum for each element is unique, providing a powerful and much used analytical tool, and many line spectra were well known for many years before they could be explained with physics. (credit for (b): Yttrium91, Wikimedia Commons)

A schematic of the hydrogen spectrum shows several series named for those who contributed most to their determination. Part of the Balmer series is in the visible spectrum, while the Lyman series is entirely in the UV, and the Paschen series and others are in the IR. Values of n_f and n_i are shown for some of the lines.

(Figure 30.16) The planetary model of the atom, as modified by Bohr, has the orbits of the electrons quantized. Only certain orbits are allowed, explaining why atomic spectra are discrete (quantized). The energy carried away from an atom by a photon comes from the electron dropping from one allowed orbit to another and is thus quantized. This is likewise true for atomic absorption of photons. (Figure 30.17) An energy-level diagram plots energy vertically and is useful in visualizing the energy states of a system and the transitions between them. This diagram is for the hydrogen-atom electrons, showing a transition between two orbits having energies E₄ and E₂. (Figure 30.18) The allowed electron orbits in hydrogen have the radii shown. These radii were first calculated by Bohr and are given by the equation r_n = (n²/Z)a_B. The lowest orbit has the experimentally verified diameter of a hydrogen atom. (Figure 30.19) Energy-level diagram for hydrogen showing the Lyman, Balmer, and Paschen series of transitions. The orbital energies are calculated using the above equation, first derived by Bohr.

exercises.prompt: A hypothetical one-electron atom in its highest excited state can only emit photons of energy $2E$, $3E$, and $5E$ before reaching the ground state. Which of the following represents the complete set of energy levels for this atom?

answer.hint: Each photon carries the difference between two levels, $\kdE = \kEini - \kEfin$. Check which set of levels gives exactly the three differences $2E$, $3E$ and $5E$.

exercises.prompt: The Lyman series of photons each have an energy capable of exciting the electron of a hydrogen atom from the ground state (energy level 1) to energy levels 2, 3, 4, etc. The wavelengths of the first five photons in this series are 121.6 nm, 102.6 nm, 97.3 nm, 95.0 nm, and 93.8 nm. The ground state energy of hydrogen is −13.6 eV. Based on the wavelengths of the Lyman series, calculate the energies of the first five excited states above ground level for a hydrogen atom to the nearest 0.1 eV.

answer.solution: Each Lyman photon is absorbed by an electron in the ground state and lifts it to a higher level, so its energy equals the difference between that level and the ground state. Find each photon’s energy from its wavelength with $E = h\kc/\klam$, using $h\kc = 1240$ eV·nm, and add it to the ground-state energy, −13.6 eV, to get the energy of the level it reaches. The first photon reaches the level $n = 2$, the second $n = 3$, and so on. Comparing the five energies with $\kEn = -13.6\ \text{eV}/n^{2}$ checks the arithmetic.

exercises.prompt: The ground state of a certain type of atom has energy $-E_0$. What is the wavelength of a photon with enough energy to ionize an atom in the ground state and give the ejected electron a kinetic energy of $2E_0$?

answer.hint: The photon must supply $E_0$ to free the electron and $2E_0$ more as kinetic energy; then $\klam = h\kc/E$.

exercises.prompt: An electron in a hydrogen atom is initially in energy level 2 ($E_2 = -3.4$ eV). (a) What frequency of photon must be absorbed by the atom in order for the electron to transition to energy level 3 ($E_3 = -1.5$ eV)? (b) What frequency of photon must be emitted by the atom in order for the electron to transition to energy level 1 ($E_1 = -13.6$ eV)?

answer.solution: (a) In absorption the atom gains exactly the energy between the two levels, $\kdE = E_3 - E_2$, from the values given. The photon carries that energy, $h\kf = \kdE$, so its frequency is $\kf = \kdE/h$ with $h = 4.14\times 10^{-15}$ eV·s. (b) In emission from level 2 to level 1 the atom loses $\kdE = E_2 - E_1$, and the emitted photon’s frequency is again that energy divided by $h$. The drop to level 1 is much larger, so the frequency in (b) is much higher, in the ultraviolet.

exercises.prompt: How do the allowed orbits for electrons in atoms differ from the allowed orbits for planets around the sun? Explain how the correspondence principle applies here.

answer.solution: An electron in an atom may occupy only certain orbits, whose radii and energies are fixed by the quantization of its angular momentum, $\kL = nh/2\pi$, so it changes orbit only by jumping from one to another and gaining or losing a definite amount of energy. A planet can have any orbit given the proper energy. Its angular momentum is also a whole multiple of $h/2\pi$, but $n$ is so enormous that neighboring allowed orbits differ by an immeasurably small amount, and the orbits appear continuous. This is the correspondence principle: for large quantum numbers the quantum description agrees with classical physics.

exercises.prompt: Explain how Bohr’s rule for the quantization of electron orbital angular momentum differs from the actual rule.

answer.solution: Bohr’s rule makes the orbital angular momentum a whole multiple of $h/2\pi$, $\kL = nh/2\pi$, with the same $n$ that labels the orbit’s energy, so it is never zero. In the full quantum mechanical description, met later in this chapter, its magnitude is set by a separate quantum number $l$, $\kL = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\,h/2\pi$ with $l = 0, 1, \ldots, n - 1$. It is then not a whole multiple of $h/2\pi$, and it is zero for every state with $l = 0$, including the ground state of hydrogen.

exercises.prompt: What is a hydrogen-like atom, and how are the energies and radii of its electron orbits related to those in hydrogen?

answer.solution: A hydrogen-like atom is any atom with only a single electron, such as He⁺ or C⁵⁺. Its nucleus has charge $Z\kqe$, so the electron is held more strongly than in hydrogen. Its orbit radii are hydrogen’s divided by $Z$, $\krn = (n^{2}/Z)\kaB$, and its orbital energies are hydrogen’s multiplied by $Z^{2}$, $\kEn = -(Z^{2}/n^{2})\kEobohr$. Its orbits are smaller and more tightly bound, and its spectrum is shifted to higher photon energies.

exercises.prompt: Atomic and molecular spectra are discrete. What does discrete mean, and how are discrete spectra related to the quantization of energy and electron orbits in atoms and molecules?

answer.solution: Discrete means made of separate values with gaps between them, rather than a continuous range. An atom’s spectrum contains only certain wavelengths, a set of separate lines. Each line is a photon whose energy $h\kf$ equals the difference between two allowed energies, $\kdE = \kEini - \kEfin$. Because the electron orbits, and so their energies, are quantized, only certain differences are possible, and only certain photon energies and wavelengths are emitted or absorbed. Molecules have quantized energies too, so their spectra are discrete as well.

exercises.prompt: Hydrogen gas can only absorb EM radiation that has an energy corresponding to a transition in the atom, just as it can only emit these discrete energies. When a spectrum is taken of the solar corona, in which a broad range of EM wavelengths are passed through very hot hydrogen gas, the absorption spectrum shows all the features of the emission spectrum. But when such EM radiation passes through room-temperature hydrogen gas, only the Lyman series is absorbed. Explain the difference.

answer.solution: Absorption lifts an electron from the level it is in to a higher one, so the lines absorbed are the transitions that start on an occupied level. In room-temperature hydrogen nearly every atom is in its ground state, $n = 1$, since the thermal energy of a few hundredths of an eV is far too small to lift an electron the 10.2 eV to $n = 2$. Only transitions that start at $n = 1$ can be absorbed, and those are the Lyman series. In the very hot corona, collisions keep many atoms in excited states, $n = 2$, 3 and higher, so transitions that start on those levels are absorbed as well, and the absorption spectrum shows the Balmer, Paschen and other series of the emission spectrum.

exercises.prompt: By calculating its wavelength, show that the first line in the Lyman series is UV radiation.

answer.hint: The first Lyman line has $n_{\text{f}} = 1$ and $n_{\text{i}} = 2$; use $1/\klam = R(1/n_{\text{f}}^{2} - 1/n_{\text{i}}^{2})$.
answer.solution: $\frac{1}{\klam} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_{\text{f}}^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_{\text{i}}^{2}}\right) \Rightarrow \klam = \frac{1}{R}\left[\frac{(n_{\text{i}}\cdot n_{\text{f}})^{2}}{n_{\text{i}}^{2} - n_{\text{f}}^{2}}\right];\ n_{\text{i}} = 2,\ n_{\text{f}} = 1$, so that $\klam = \left(\frac{\text{m}}{1.097\times 10^{7}}\right)\left[\frac{(2\times 1)^{2}}{2^{2} - 1^{2}}\right] = 1.22\times 10^{-7}\;\text{m} = 122\;\text{nm}$, which is UV radiation.

exercises.prompt: Look up the values of the quantities in $\kaB = \frac{h^{2}}{4\pi^{2} m_{\text{e}} k \kqe^{2}}$, and verify that the Bohr radius $\kaB$ is $0.529\times 10^{-10}\;\text{m}$.
If a hydrogen atom has its electron in the $n = 4$ state, how much energy in eV is needed to ionize it?

answer.hint: The electron is free at zero energy, so the energy needed is the size of $\kEn = -13.6\ \text{eV}/n^{2}$ at $n = 4$.

exercises.prompt: Find the radius of a hydrogen atom in the $n = 2$ state according to Bohr’s theory.
What is the smallest-wavelength line in the Balmer series? Is it in the visible part of the spectrum?

answer.hint: The shortest wavelength is the series limit, $n_{\text{i}} \to \infty$, so $1/\klam = R/n_{\text{f}}^{2}$ with $n_{\text{f}} = 2$.
answer.solution:
365 nm

It is in the ultraviolet.

exercises.prompt: Do the Balmer and Lyman series overlap? To answer this, calculate the shortest-wavelength Balmer line and the longest-wavelength Lyman line.
A wavelength of $4.653\;\mu\text{m}$ is observed in a hydrogen spectrum for a transition that ends in the $n_{\text{f}} = 5$ level. What was $n_{\text{i}}$ for the initial level of the electron?

answer.hint: Solve $1/\klam = R(1/n_{\text{f}}^{2} - 1/n_{\text{i}}^{2})$ for $1/n_{\text{i}}^{2}$ and round $n_{\text{i}}$ to the nearest whole number.

exercises.prompt: A beryllium ion with a single electron (denoted Be<sup>3+</sup>) is in an excited state with radius the same as that of the ground state of hydrogen. (a) What is $n$ for the Be<sup>3+</sup> ion? (b) How much energy in eV is needed to ionize the ion from this excited state?

parts.hint: The energy needed is the size of $\kEn = -(Z^{2}/n^{2})(13.6\ \text{eV})$.

exercises.prompt: Verify Equations $\krn = \frac{n^{2}}{Z}\kaB$ and $\kaB = \frac{h^{2}}{4\pi^{2} m_{\text{e}} k \kqe^{2}} = 0.529\times 10^{-10}\;\text{m}$ using the approach stated in the text. That is, equate the Coulomb and centripetal forces and then insert an expression for velocity from the condition for angular momentum quantization.

answer.solution: $\frac{kZq_{e}^{2}}{r_{n}^{2}} = \frac{m_{e}V^{2}}{r_{n}}$, so that $r_{n} = \frac{kZq_{e}^{2}}{m_{e}V^{2}} = \frac{kZq_{e}^{2}}{m_{e}}\frac{1}{V^{2}}$. From the equation $m_{e}vr_{n} = n\frac{h}{2\pi}$, we can substitute for the velocity, giving: $r_{n} = \frac{kZq_{e}^{2}}{m_{e}}\cdot\frac{4\pi^{2}m_{e}^{2}r_{n}^{2}}{n^{2}h^{2}}$ so that $r_{n} = \frac{n^{2}}{Z}\frac{h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}m_{e}kq_{e}^{2}} = \frac{n^{2}}{Z}a_{\text{B}}$, where $a_{\text{B}} = \frac{h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}m_{e}kq_{e}^{2}}$.

exercises.prompt: A galaxy moving away from the earth has a speed of $0.0100c$. What wavelength do we observe for an $n_{\text{i}} = 7$ to $n_{\text{f}} = 2$ transition for hydrogen in that galaxy?

answer.hint: Find the emitted wavelength from $1/\klam = R(1/n_{\text{f}}^{2} - 1/n_{\text{i}}^{2})$, then apply the Doppler shift for a source receding at $0.0100c$, which lengthens it.

exercises.prompt: A pulsar is a rapidly spinning remnant of a supernova. It rotates on its axis, sweeping hydrogen along with it so that hydrogen on one side moves toward us as fast as 50.0 km/s, while that on the other side moves away as fast as 50.0 km/s. This means that the EM radiation we receive will be Doppler shifted over a range of $\pm 50.0$ km/s. What range of wavelengths will we observe for the 91.20-nm line in the Lyman series of hydrogen? (Such line broadening is observed and actually provides part of the evidence for rapid rotation.)

parts.hint: Hydrogen moving toward us at 50.0 km/s shortens the wavelength by the fraction $\kv/\kc$.
Hydrogen moving away at 50.0 km/s lengthens the wavelength by the fraction $\kv/\kc$.

exercises.prompt: Particles called muons exist in cosmic rays and can be created in particle accelerators. Muons are very similar to electrons, having the same charge and spin, but they have a mass 207 times greater. When muons are captured by an atom, they orbit just like an electron but with a smaller radius, since the mass in $\kaB = \frac{h^{2}}{4\pi^{2} m_{\text{e}} k \kqe^{2}} = 0.529\times 10^{-10}\;\text{m}$ is $207\,m_{\text{e}}$. (a) Calculate the radius of the $n = 1$ orbit for a muon in a uranium ion ($Z = 92$). (b) Compare this with the 7.5-fm radius of a uranium nucleus. Note that since the muon orbits inside the electron, it falls into a hydrogen-like orbit. Since your answer is less than the radius of the nucleus, you can see that the photons emitted as the muon falls into its lowest orbit can give information about the nucleus.

parts.part: (a) the radius of the n = 1 orbit
parts.hint: Divide the Bohr radius by 207 for the muon’s mass and by $Z = 92$ for the nucleus, $\krn = (n^{2}/Z)\kaB$.

parts.part: (b) the orbit radius as a fraction of the nuclear radius
parts.hint: Divide the radius from (a) by 7.5 fm.

exercises.prompt: (a) For carbon, calculate the energy when an electron falls from $n = 3$ to $n = 2$, then from $n = 2$ to $n = 1$. Then add these for the total energy released in the process. (b) Calculate the energy released when the electron falls directly from $n = 3$ to $n = 1$. (c) Are the energies in part a and in part b the same?

parts.part: (a) the energy from n = 3 to n = 2
parts.hint: A carbon ion with one electron has $Z = 6$; use $\kEn = -(Z^{2}/n^{2})(13.6\ \text{eV})$.

parts.part: (a) the energy from n = 2 to n = 1
(b) the energy from n = 3 to n = 1
